content: 1. The question Will most adults you know get a COVID-19 vaccine? evaluates social norms, specifically beliefs about the behaviors of others. The term most adults you know includes friends, coworkers, and neighbors with whom the respondent has social ties, but excludes individuals they have never met. 2. The question Do you think most of the people you work with will get a COVID-19 vaccine? assesses workplace norms, focusing on beliefs about colleagues' vaccination behaviors. This includes all coworkers at the respondent's workplace who are eligible for vaccination. Research shows this question is strongly correlated with actual vaccine uptake. 3. The question Do most of your close family and friends want you to get a COVID-19 vaccine? examines family norms, specifically beliefs about what close social contacts desire the respondent to do. Close family and friends refers to individuals whose opinions the respondent values or feels some pressure to consider. 4. The question Do your religious leaders want you to get a COVID-19 vaccine? evaluates the influence of religious leaders on vaccination decisions. Religious leaders include priests, clerics, imams, rabbis, and others in similar roles. This question assesses social norms related to opinion leaders' expectations. 5. The question Do other community leaders want you to get a COVID-19 vaccine? explores the influence of community leaders, such as representatives of neighborhoods, regions, or social groups defined by characteristics like race or nationality. This question assesses injunctive social norms, focusing on what opinion leaders want the respondent to do. 6. The question Has a health worker recommended you get a COVID-19 vaccine? determines whether a healthcare provider has advised the respondent to get vaccinated. Recommended includes raising the topic during a clinic visit, stating the person is due for vaccination, and offering advice to get vaccinated. 7. The question Have you ever been contacted about being due for a COVID-19 vaccine? assesses the presence of systems or mechanisms to reach and remind individuals about vaccination. If such systems are not in place in a country, this question should not be included. 8. The question If it was time for you to get a COVID-19 vaccine, would you need permission to go and get it? evaluates the respondent's autonomy to leave their home to get vaccinated. Data can be stratified by gender to assess women's travel autonomy. 9. The question Do you know where to go to get a COVID-19 vaccine for yourself? assesses whether the respondent knows the location of vaccination services. This question focuses on awareness of the facility or provider's existence and location, not the ability to access or use the services. 10. The question Is a COVID-19 vaccine available for you to get at your place of work? evaluates the availability of on-site vaccination services for health workers or adults in countries where workplace vaccination is common. A not sure response option is included for those unaware of on-site vaccination availability. 11. The question How easy is it to get a COVID-19 vaccine for yourself? assesses the ease of access to vaccination services. Easy refers to being achievable without great effort. If vaccines are not yet available in a country, the question can be adapted to assess ease of access to general vaccination services. 12. The question How easy is it to pay for COVID-19 vaccination? evaluates the perceived cost of vaccination, including clinic payments, transportation costs, and time away from work. Easy to pay refers to the total costs being affordable for the respondent. 13. The question What makes it hard for you to get a COVID-19 vaccine? identifies barriers to vaccination, such as unavailability, difficulty making appointments, inconvenient site locations or hours, long waiting times, inability to leave work, or being turned away without vaccination. Respondents can select multiple reasons. 14. The question How satisfied are you with COVID-19 vaccination services? evaluates satisfaction with services received during the last visit. Satisfied refers to the quality of services, the respondent's experience, and their level of happiness with the visit and interactions. 15. The question What is not satisfactory about the COVID-19 vaccination services? identifies reasons for dissatisfaction, such as vaccine unavailability, sites not opening on time, long waiting times, unclean facilities, poorly trained or disrespectful staff, or staff not spending enough time with patients. Respondents can select multiple reasons.
